key_insight: Inverse PINNs can estimate Manning friction reliably only when observations are sufficiently dense, low-noise, and include both depth and velocity; otherwise, identifiability breaks down.
engineering_relevance: This benchmark helps determine when physics-informed inverse models are trustworthy for shallow-water calibration from sparse field data, and when conventional data assimilation or additional measurements are needed.
method: Benchmarked inverse PINNs on two shallow-water cases: 1D MacDonald channel and 2D sloped channel.
Treated Manning friction as a positive trainable scalar learned jointly with the flow field.
Used a two-phase training strategy: fit observations first, then enforce physics residuals.
evidence_signal: In the 2D case, friction error stayed below 5% with at least 10 observations and noise up to 10% of field standard deviation, while the 1D case retained a ~15% positive bias regardless of sparsity or noise.
watch_item: Results depend strongly on observing both depth and velocity; using only one variable or too few points can make the inverse estimate unreliable.
paper_title: How Sparse and How Noisy? Systematic Benchmarking of Inverse Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Manning Friction Estimation in Shallow Water Equations
